feed.title: I build World Models. Tumors break them.
feed.subtitle: We build generalizable, uncertainty-aware world models for tumor evolution and metastasis, models that (i) learn causal/functional links from genotype to regulatory state to phenotype, (ii) explicitly represent measurement noise and batch effects in real sequencing data, and (iii) transfer across cancers, tissues, and platforms. The scientific payoff is how somatic/germline variation rewires regulatory programs, how early genetic events bias invasive and metastatic routes, and how chromosomal instability (CIN) and tumor-intrinsic programs enable organ-specific colonization. The translational payoff is cheaper, scalable profiling and cleaner data, enabling robust biomarkers and therapeutic hypotheses.

entry.title: Developmental and MAPK-responsive cell states in pancreatic cancer

link.title: Developmental and MAPK-responsive cell states in pancreatic cancer

entry.content:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma contains malignant epithelial cells in multiple molecular states. A central question is whether these states reflect a single continuum or distinct regulatory programs with different biological dependencies.

In this study, single-cell master-regulator analysis across multiple cohorts identified three co-existing developmental lineage states: a poorly differentiated state associated with epithelial–mesenchymal-transition regulators and two well-differentiated states associated with gastrointestinal and pancreatic developmental programs. Each lineage also separated into low- and high-MAPK substates, revealing an additional layer of epigenetic organization.

This state map connects tumor-cell identity to histopathology, spatial organization, plasticity, and genetic dependencies. It provides a framework for asking which regulatory programs maintain each malignant state and where state-selective therapeutic vulnerabilities may emerge.

Journal: Nature Genetics (2026)
Article: doi:10.1038/s41588-026-02714-8
entry.summary: Distinct developmental lineages and MAPK-responsive substates reveal state-specific dependencies in pancreatic cancer.

entry.title: Human-centered agentic AI for biomedical research

link.title: Human-centered agentic AI for biomedical research

entry.content:
Agentic AI can do more than generate text: it can plan analyses, use tools, synthesize evidence, and propose next steps. In biomedical research, however, useful autonomy must remain coupled to scientific accountability.

This framework organizes the problem around three linked ideas:

  • scientific agency — what an AI system may plan or execute, and where human judgment remains essential;
  • evidence — how claims retain traceable support, uncertainty, and reproducible provenance; and
  • governance — how permissions, oversight, and responsibility should scale with the consequence of an action.

The goal is not autonomy for its own sake. It is a human-centered research architecture in which agents help scientists move faster while preserving inspectability, methodological rigor, and clear decision ownership.

Framework: Zenodo (2026)
Record: doi:10.5281/zenodo.22100167
entry.summary: A framework for scientific agency, evidence, and governance in biomedical AI.

entry.title: CXCR4 inhibition and chemoimmunotherapy in metastatic pancreatic cancer

link.title: CXCR4 inhibition and chemoimmunotherapy in metastatic pancreatic cancer

entry.content:
The CXCR4–CXCL12 axis contributes to immune exclusion in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. This study tested whether disrupting that axis could support an immune response when combined with PD-1 blockade and standard chemotherapy.

The first stage of an open-label, single-arm phase 2 trial evaluated motixafortide, cemiplimab, gemcitabine, and nab-paclitaxel in 11 treatment-naïve patients with metastatic disease. The reported objective response rate was 64%, with 55% confirmed partial responses and a 91% disease-control rate. Median progression-free and overall survival were 9.7 and 10.1 months, respectively.

Single-cell correlatives are especially important here: they connect the clinical intervention to changes in the tumor ecosystem and help clarify which immune and tumor states accompany response. The results are encouraging but should be interpreted in the context of the study’s small, non-randomized first stage.

Journal: Nature Communications (2026)
Article: doi:10.1038/s41467-026-76559-4
entry.summary: A phase 2 study combines motixafortide, cemiplimab, and chemotherapy with single-cell correlatives.

entry.title: Organ-specific colonization and niche remodeling in a human tissue model

link.title: Organ-specific colonization and niche remodeling in a human tissue model

entry.content:
Metastatic cells must survive transit, enter distant tissues, and adapt to microenvironments that differ profoundly across organs. Human experimental systems that preserve these organ-specific interactions are therefore essential for studying colonization directly.

This work established a multitissue model in which engineered bone and lung tissues are linked by vascular flow containing circulating cancer cells. Parental breast-cancer cells colonized both tissues and acquired local transcriptional programs, with particularly strong adaptation after homing to bone.

Bone- and lung-tropic derivatives retained organ-specific behavior in independently perfused platforms. Bone-tropic cells produced stronger bone colonization and osteolysis, whereas lung-tropic cells caused greater disruption of lung epithelium. The system creates a bridge between mechanistic tissue engineering and computational models of metastatic state transitions.

Journal: Science Translational Medicine (2026)
Article: doi:10.1126/scitranslmed.adv6871
entry.summary: A vascularized bone-and-lung platform models how disseminated tumor cells adapt to organ-specific niches.

entry.title: Endothelial ICAM-1 polarization and T-cell exclusion in melanoma

link.title: Endothelial ICAM-1 polarization and T-cell exclusion in melanoma

entry.content:
Antitumor immunity depends not only on whether T cells are present, but also on whether they can reach malignant cells inside the tumor. This preprint examines a vascular mechanism that helps determine that spatial access.

Endothelial cells isolated from tumor cores and margins identified ICAM-1 as a candidate regulator of T-cell localization. As tumors grew, T cells became excluded from the core while endothelial ICAM-1 became enriched at the periphery. Blocking ICAM-1 restored intratumoral T-cell infiltration, increased effector activity, delayed growth of immunogenic tumors, and sensitized an immune-refractory model to anti-PD-1 therapy.

The findings position the endothelial ICAM-1/LFA-1 axis as a spatial checkpoint in the tumor microenvironment. They also show why spatially resolved analysis can reveal mechanisms that are obscured when immune abundance is measured without location.

Preprint: bioRxiv (2026)
Article: doi:10.64898/2026.03.19.712709
entry.summary: Spatial organization of the tumor vasculature emerges as a modifiable regulator of T-cell access.

entry.title: Chromosomal instability reshapes the esophageal cancer microenvironment

link.title: Chromosomal instability reshapes the esophageal cancer microenvironment

entry.content:
Chromosomal instability is common in esophageal adenocarcinoma and is associated with aggressive disease. Although micronuclei generated by instability can activate cGAS–STING signaling, that activation does not necessarily produce an effective antitumor immune response.

Across experimental models and human tumors, this study links ongoing chromosomal instability to tumor-intrinsic innate immune signaling, chemokine production, and myeloid-cell recruitment. CXCL8 emerged as a prominent conserved output of this program. The analysis combines whole-genome sequencing, single-nucleus RNA sequencing, multiplex immunophenotyping, and in situ measurement of cGAS-positive micronuclei.

The results illustrate how a genome-level process can remodel the surrounding ecosystem. They also motivate models that connect copy-number dynamics and micronuclei to signaling, cellular composition, and therapeutic response rather than treating chromosomal instability as a single static score.

Journal: Science Advances (2026)
Article: doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeb1611
entry.summary: A cGAS–chemokine–myeloid axis links ongoing chromosomal instability to immune remodeling.

entry.title: Pan-cancer inference and validation of hypermorphic, hypomorphic and neomorphic mutations

link.title: Pan-cancer inference and validation of hypermorphic, hypomorphic and neomorphic mutations

entry.content:
Mutations in cancer genes do not all behave the same way. While many are broadly classified as gain-of-function or loss-of-function, the functional consequences of mutations are often more nuanced.

In this work, we developed a computational framework to systematically infer hypermorphic, hypomorphic, and neomorphic mutations across diverse cancer types. By integrating large-scale genomic and transcriptomic datasets, we identified mutations that increase gene activity, partially reduce function, or generate entirely new molecular behavior.

The study combines computational prediction with experimental validation to demonstrate that these functional mutation classes can reshape regulatory networks in distinct ways. Our findings highlight the importance of moving beyond simple binary classifications of mutations and instead recognizing the diverse spectrum of functional effects that mutations can produce.

Understanding these mutation classes provides a more precise framework for interpreting cancer genomes and may help guide therapeutic strategies that target specific functional alterations.

Journal: Nature Genetics (2026)
entry.summary: Understanding functional mutation classes across cancers.

entry.title: Cellular states associated with metastatic organotropism and survival in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma

link.title: Cellular states associated with metastatic organotropism and survival in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma

entry.content:
Metastasis is responsible for the majority of cancer-related deaths, yet the biological programs that determine where tumors spread remain poorly understood.

In this study, we analyzed large-scale single-cell transcriptomic data from pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) to identify tumor cell states associated with metastatic organotropism. By integrating transcriptional programs with clinical outcomes, we uncovered cellular states that correlate with both metastatic patterns and patient survival.

These findings suggest that metastatic behavior is not solely determined by genetic alterations, but also by the transcriptional states adopted by tumor cells. Distinct cellular programs appear to predispose tumors to colonize specific organs and influence disease progression.

The work provides new insight into the relationship between tumor cell plasticity, metastatic dissemination, and clinical outcomes in PDAC.

Journal: Nature Genetics (2025)
entry.summary: Single-cell analysis reveals tumor programs linked to metastatic spread.

entry.title: Chromosomal instability and neural-like programs in NSCLC brain metastasis

link.title: Chromosomal instability and neural-like programs in NSCLC brain metastasis

entry.content:
This post highlights our recent work on non-small cell lung cancer brain metastasis.

Using multi-modal single-cell and spatial profiling, we found that brain metastases are characterized by pronounced chromosomal instability and neural-like transcriptional programs. Rather than simply reconstructing tumor evolution, this study focused on identifying biological features that distinguish metastatic tumors from primary lesions and may help explain metastatic fitness in the brain microenvironment.

Key themes from this work include:

  • chromosomal instability as a major feature of metastatic biology,
  • neural-like state programs in metastatic tumor cells,
  • integration of single-cell and spatial transcriptomic data,
  • implications for biomarker discovery and therapeutic targeting.

Citation: Tagore S, et al. PMID: 40016452
entry.summary: Highlights from our multi-modal single-cell and spatial study of brain metastasis.

entry.title: Welcome to my research blog
entry.content:
Welcome to my research blog.

I use this space to share brief updates on my work in cancer genomics, single-cell and spatial biology, and AI-based world models for tumor evolution and metastasis.

My research focuses on how genomic alterations reshape regulatory programs, how early events bias metastatic trajectories, and how uncertainty-aware computational models can improve biological discovery and translation.

Here I will post:

  • research updates,
  • method development notes,
  • publication highlights,
  • grant and project ideas,
  • and perspectives on computational oncology.

Thank you for visiting.
entry.summary: Research notes on cancer genomics, single-cell biology, and AI-driven modeling.
